Mobile system design, from a packet to an app · Puzzle 1 · 2 of 11

Finding the server

Puzzle 0 said every packet carries an address. Your code never writes one: it writes a name like api.example.com. Here's how the phone turns that name into a number, and what that costs.

Builds on: open one to see the idea this puzzle uses.

  • Puzzle 0: What actually travels

    Data crosses the internet in packets. IP addresses each packet and routes it, but can lose, delay or reorder it. TCP turns those packets into a reliable, ordered stream: it numbers them, waits for acknowledgements and resends what's lost, and needs a connection set up first. TLS encrypts that stream, and HTTP is the language of requests and responses on top.

The problem

Your Retrofit base URL is https://api.example.com. Puzzle 0 said IP delivers packets by address. A name isn't an address. So before the first packet can leave, something has to turn the name into a number. What, and how long does it take?

See it

Save this diagram as a GIF

The building block

Every machine reachable on the internet has an IP address: a number, like 93.184.215.14, that routers read to deliver each packet.

Numbers are hard to remember and change when a company moves servers, so people and code use a hostname instead: api.example.com.

DNS, the Domain Name System, is the internet's phone book: a worldwide system of servers that answers "which address does this hostname have?". Before your app's first connection to a host, the phone sends that question and waits for the answer.

Two consequences for an app:

  • The very first request to a host waits for a DNS answer first: more waiting before anything useful happens.
  • The answer is cached: kept for a while by the phone (and by DNS servers on the way), so the next requests skip the lookup.

The analogy

Looking up a friend's number in your contacts before you can call. The first time, you search; after that, the number's on your recent calls list.

Check yourself

Your app's first-ever request to api.example.com is slower than the next ones. Which part of that is DNS?

Right. Name to address, once.

Not quite. Routers deliver by address; the name is resolved by DNS first.

Not quite. The data is the same size; the extra wait is the lookup before sending.

Why are DNS answers cached?

Right. Look up once, reuse.

Not quite. Packets always need an address; caching only keeps it.

Not quite. They answer many times; caching saves the wait.

What's the difference between a hostname and an IP address?

Not quite. That's the two swapped. Re-read that part ↑

Right. Name vs number.

Sources

  • MDN: DNS ("DNS (Domain Name System) is a hierarchical and decentralized naming system for Internet-connected resources. DNS maintains a list of domain names along with the resources, such as IP addresses, that are associated with them.")

What you now know

Every machine on the internet has an IP address, a number that routers use to deliver packets. People and code use hostnames instead, like api.example.com. Before the first connection, the phone asks DNS, the internet's phone book, which address a hostname has. That lookup is one more round trip on a cold start, so the answer is cached for a while.
